extra.message: Overly Broad Internal Ops Router Exposed with Static Token Only — A single leaked or brute-forced static token grants access to multiple critical-severity attack vectors including RCE, SSRF, and arbitrary file read/write. [verified: The entire `/ops/*` router is protected solely by a static shared-secret header with no user authentication, IP restriction, rate limiting, or audit logging; any caller who obtains `INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN` gains access to RCE (shell, jinja, dock), SSRF (relay), XXE (xml), and arbitrary file read/write (parcel, vault) endpoints. This is a genuine missing-control finding confirmed by the code.]

Path Traversal and Sensitive Data Stored Plaintext via /ops/vault Endpoint — Attacker can write files to arbitrary server locations and persist cleartext financial/PII data (SSN, card numbers) on disk. [verified: Duplicate of idx 6 — the `/ops/vault/tenant-stash-242` endpoint writes a JSON file with plaintext SSN and card number to `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / f'{ref}.json'` where `ref` is caller-controlled without sanitization, confirmed path traversal + plaintext PII storage, gated only by the static ops token.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) in jinja endpoint — Remote code execution; complete server compromise, credential theft, data exfiltration. [verified: The `/ops/jinja/tenant-cast-581` endpoint constructs `Template('Result: ' + fragment).render()` with caller-controlled `fragment` using the standard (non-sandboxed) Jinja2 environment, enabling full SSTI RCE. Gate is only the static ops token.]

OS Command Injection via ping host parameter — Remote code execution as the application user; full server compromise, data exfiltration, lateral movement. [verified: At line 62 (actual line in file: the `/ops/shell/tenant-probe-631` endpoint), `_os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host)` concatenates the attacker-controlled `host` query parameter directly into a shell command with no sanitization. The only gate is the static `INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN` header check, which is a shared secret with no per-user auth, rate limiting, or IP restriction.]

XML External Entity (XXE) Injection — Arbitrary local file read (e.g., /etc/passwd, application config), SSRF to internal services, potential denial of service via recursive entity expansion. [verified: The `/ops/xml/tenant-fold-621` endpoint constructs `etree.XMLParser(load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False)` and parses the raw request body, enabling full XXE for local file read and SSRF. No input validation exists beyond the ops token gate.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 Template Construction — Remote code execution; full server compromise via Jinja2 sandbox escape. [verified: Duplicate of idx 2 — the `/ops/jinja/tenant-cast-581` endpoint constructs an unsandboxed Jinja2 `Template('Result: ' + fragment).render()` with caller-controlled `fragment`, confirmed SSTI leading to RCE, gated only by the static ops token.]

XML External Entity (XXE) Injection in /ops/xml Endpoint — Arbitrary local file read, SSRF to internal services, potential RCE depending on lxml version. [verified: Duplicate of idx 3 — the `/ops/xml/tenant-fold-621` endpoint uses `etree.XMLParser(load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False)` on caller-supplied body, confirmed full XXE enabling local file read and SSRF, gated only by the static ops token.]

OS Command Injection via `host` Parameter in /ops/shell Endpoint — Remote code execution as the application user; full server compromise, data exfiltration, lateral movement. [verified: Duplicate of idx 0 — the `/ops/shell/tenant-probe-631` endpoint at the actual shell line concatenates the caller-controlled `host` into `_os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host)` with no sanitization; confirmed OS command injection gated only by the static ops token.]

Password Reset Token Returned in API Response Body — Attacker who intercepts or reads the API response (via XSS, shared browser, network interception) obtains a valid reset token and can take over any user account whose email they supply. [verified: The full raw reset token is returned in the API response body at line 126 (`mock_email_token`), confirmed to be displayed to the user by the frontend (main.jsx line 117); this entirely bypasses the email-verification step and the token suffix is additionally logged in the audit record, both constituting real sensitive data exposures.]

Password Reset Token Exposed in API Response — Attacker can take over any account by immediately using the returned reset token, bypassing the entire email-verification flow. [verified: Line 126 of auth.py unconditionally returns `raw_token` (the full 43-char password-reset token) in the JSON response body as `mock_email_token`; no transport security (cookie uses secure=False allowing plaintext HTTP) and no mechanism prevents any observer or the requester themselves from immediately using this token to reset any targeted account's password without email access.]

Session Cookie Transmitted Over Plaintext HTTP (secure=False) — Session hijacking; an attacker on the network path captures the session cookie and impersonates any user including admins. [verified: In `create_session` (security.py line 58–66), `secure=False` is hardcoded unconditionally on the session cookie, meaning the browser will transmit it over plaintext HTTP. No configuration override or TLS-enforcement middleware exists to compensate.]

Path Traversal in tenant-boxfile-pull endpoint — Arbitrary file read; attacker can exfiltrate application secrets, configuration files, SSH keys, database credentials, and other sensitive data. [verified: The `/ops/parcel/tenant-boxfile-pull-086` endpoint constructs `parcel_path = BASE_EXPORT_DIR / packet_ref` from the caller-controlled query parameter and calls `read_text()` on it with no path canonicalization or parent-directory check, allowing `../../etc/passwd` style traversal. Only the ops token gates this.]

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in relay endpoints — Attacker can probe and read responses from internal services unreachable from the internet, including cloud metadata endpoints, internal databases, admin interfaces, and other microservices. [verified: The `/ops/relay/lease-meter-card-087` endpoint at line 40 passes the caller-controlled `url` parameter directly to `urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=3)` with no URL scheme or host allow-list. The only barrier is the static ops token; any token holder can reach internal metadata services or localhost ports.]

NoSQL Injection in MongoDB query endpoint — Attacker can bypass query logic, enumerate all records in the MongoDB ops.records collection, and potentially execute arbitrary JavaScript via $where operator. [verified: The `/ops/mongo/tenant-lane-611` endpoint passes `payload.get('filter', payload)` — a fully attacker-controlled dict — directly to `find_one(query)` with no sanitization, enabling MongoDB operator injection (`$where`, `$regex`, `$gt`) to bypass query logic or execute arbitrary JS. Only the ops token gates this.]

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via Caller-Controlled URL in /ops/relay Endpoints — Access to cloud metadata services, internal network scanning, credential theft from instance metadata (AWS/GCP/Azure). [verified: Duplicate of idx 1/11 — both relay endpoints (`/ops/relay/lease-meter-card-087` and `/ops/relay/tenant-probe-357`) pass fully attacker-controlled URL/endpoint parameters to `urllib.request.urlopen` with no scheme or host allow-list, confirmed SSRF gated only by the static ops token.]

NoSQL Injection via Unvalidated MongoDB Filter Object — Bypass MongoDB query logic, extract arbitrary records, or cause denial of service via long-running queries. [verified: Duplicate of idx 12 — the `/ops/mongo/tenant-lane-611` endpoint passes `payload.get('filter', payload)` directly to MongoDB `find_one()` without sanitization, confirmed NoSQL injection enabling operator injection and arbitrary record extraction, gated only by the static ops token.]

Hardcoded Admin Demo Credentials in Frontend Source — Any visitor can read the JavaScript bundle, extract admin credentials, and authenticate as a property admin with full system access. [verified: config.py defaults demo_password to 'Password123!' when DEMO_PASSWORD env var is absent, and seed.py uses that value to hash and create all demo accounts including admin@mockpm.dev with role property_admin. The frontend JS bundle also hardcodes the same email/password in the useState initializer, confirming the credential is both seeded into the DB and publicly readable from the bundle.]

Hardcoded Default Secret Key and Demo Password — If APP_SECRET_KEY is not overridden in production, an attacker knowing the default can forge or predict any security tokens that depend on it; known demo password enables account takeover of seed accounts. [verified: The `demo_password` defaults to the well-known `'Password123!'` and is used to seed real user accounts (admin, manager, worker, tenant) via the seed script; if the env var is unset and the seed is run, those accounts use a publicly known password. The `app_secret_key` default is present but `app_secret_key` is never actually consumed in any cryptographic operation in the codebase (sessions use `se]

No Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints — Password brute-force attacks on any account; automated credential stuffing; account enumeration via timing side-channel. [verified: The login endpoint (line 35) and password-reset/request endpoint (line 72) have no rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA, or back-off anywhere in the codebase — no slowapi, no middleware, no decorator — confirmed by searching the entire repo; unlimited brute-force attempts are possible against any account.]

No Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints (Login and Password Reset) — Attacker can brute-force passwords for any account, or flood password-reset requests causing DoS and account harassment. [verified: No rate limiting, throttling, lockout, or CAPTCHA exists anywhere in the application (confirmed by exhaustive search); both `POST /auth/login` and `POST /auth/password-reset/request` are fully open to unlimited automated requests, enabling credential brute-force and reset-request flooding.]

Account Enumeration via Password Reset Response Difference — Attacker can enumerate all registered email addresses by calling POST /auth/password-reset/request and checking for presence of mock_email_token in response. [verified: When the email exists and the account is active the response includes `mock_email_token`; when it does not, the response is `{"ok": true}` with no such key — the code comment claims "Always return success so reset requests do not disclose account existence" but the presence/absence of `mock_email_token` in the response definitively distinguishes the two cases, making account enumeration trivially ]

CSV Formula Injection in Exported Reports — When a staff member opens an exported CSV in Excel, attacker-controlled formula cells execute, potentially exfiltrating data or running macros. [verified: All three bulk export endpoints (rent-roll, maintenance-status, inspections) write user-influenced fields (`full_name`, `category`, `findings`, `follow_up_task`, etc.) raw through `csv.DictWriter` without any formula-prefix escaping; a crafted value beginning with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` stored in the database will be interpreted as a spreadsheet formula, enabling CSV injection when staff open the f]

CSV Formula Injection in Payment Receipt Export — When a victim opens the exported CSV in Excel/LibreOffice, attacker-controlled formula cells execute, potentially exfiltrating data via HTTP requests or executing local commands via DDE. [verified: The `export_payment_receipt` endpoint writes `payment.reference`, `tenant.full_name`, and other user-influenced string fields directly into CSV via `csv.DictWriter` with no formula-prefix sanitization; a value like `=HYPERLINK(...)` stored in the DB (e.g., via CSV import or tenant registration) will execute as a formula when opened in Excel/LibreOffice. No escaping or sanitization exists in `csv_r]

Insufficient Authorization on User Listing — Tenants Can Enumerate Maintenance Workers — Any authenticated tenant can enumerate all maintenance worker accounts (names, emails, phone numbers), leaking PII and enabling targeted social engineering. [verified: Same flawed condition as idx 0 — when role='maintenance_worker' is supplied the 403 branch is never reached, confirming any authenticated tenant can retrieve names, emails, and phone numbers of all maintenance workers via GET /api/users?role=maintenance_worker.]

Sensitive Tenant Note Exposed to Property Managers — Property managers can read internal sensitive notes (e.g. legal disputes, mental health notes, background check flags) about tenants, which may be intended for admin eyes only. [verified: The `tenant_out` serializer unconditionally includes `sensitive_note` in its output and is called by `list_tenants` which grants access to both ROLE_PROPERTY_ADMIN and ROLE_PROPERTY_MANAGER with no per-field filtering. A property manager can directly call GET /tenants and receive `sensitive_note` for every tenant in the API JSON response; the frontend column suppression provides no server-side pro]

Client-Controlled content_type Used in FileResponse — Stored XSS via file download — browser executes attacker-uploaded HTML/JS if content-type is set to text/html; also enables polyglot file attacks. [verified: The `store_upload` function returns `upload.content_type` verbatim (no allowlist, no sanitization) which is then stored in `Document.content_type` and passed directly as `media_type` to `FileResponse` at documents.py line 146 — there are zero intervening controls. However, exploitability as stored XSS depends on the browser not applying X-Content-Type-Options sniff protection and the portal not se]

Unvalidated Client-Supplied Content-Type Used in File Download Response — Attacker uploads a file with Content-Type text/html; victim staff/tenant who clicks download receives and browser-renders attacker HTML, executing arbitrary JavaScript in the portal origin. [verified: Identical root cause as finding 0: `upload.content_type` flows unvalidated through `store_upload` → `Document.content_type` → `FileResponse(media_type=doc.content_type)` with no MIME allowlist, magic-byte check, or response-header override anywhere in the codebase. An attacker with upload access can force arbitrary MIME types (e.g., `text/html`) causing browsers to render downloaded files as HTML ]

Open Redirect via Caller-Controlled `lane` Parameter — Phishing campaigns; bypass referrer-based access controls; redirect after OAuth flows to attacker-controlled pages. [verified: Duplicate of idx 14 — the `/ops/after/tenant-lane-159` endpoint returns `RedirectResponse(lane)` with a fully attacker-controlled `lane` parameter and no origin validation, confirmed open redirect, gated only by the static ops token.]

Open Redirect in tenant-lane endpoint — Phishing and social engineering attacks; users following links are transparently redirected to attacker-controlled sites. [verified: The `/ops/after/tenant-lane-159` endpoint returns `RedirectResponse(lane)` where `lane` is a fully attacker-controlled query parameter with no origin restriction, enabling open redirect to arbitrary external URLs. The ops token requirement raises the bar but does not eliminate phishing risk from token holders or leaked links.]

Denial of Service via Unbounded count Parameter in Spool Endpoint — Server memory exhaustion causes application crash and denial of service for all users. [verified: The `/ops/spool/tenant-fan-314` endpoint accepts an unbounded integer `count` parameter and allocates `count` dicts in memory with no upper bound check, allowing a token holder to exhaust server memory with a single request (e.g., `count=2147483647`). This is a real DoS vector for any ops token holder.]

Weak PRNG Used for Nonce/Token Generation — Nonces generated via random.choice are predictable by an attacker who can observe previous values; if used in security-sensitive contexts this enables forgery of tokens. [verified: The `/ops/nonce/tenant-roll-601` endpoint uses `random.choice` (Mersenne Twister) rather than `secrets.choice` to generate nonce codes; if these codes are consumed by security-sensitive callers (CSRF tokens, OTP, session nonces), they are predictable after observing output samples. The vulnerability is real but impact depends on downstream use.]

Weak PRNG Used for Security Nonce Generation — Attacker can predict nonce values, undermining any security mechanism that relies on them (e.g. CSRF tokens, session IDs, OTP codes). [verified: Duplicate of idx 8 — the `/ops/nonce/tenant-roll-601` endpoint uses `random.choice` (non-CSPRNG Mersenne Twister) to generate nonces; if consumed as security tokens the values are predictable. Confirmed weak PRNG usage.]

Hardcoded Default Password in User Creation Form — Any staff account created through the UI without an explicit password is initialized to the publicly-known credential 'Password123!', enabling trivial unauthorized access to manager/worker/admin accounts. [verified: UserManagement initializes and resets form state with password='Password123!' (lines 619, 625), so any staff account created via the UI without an explicit password override silently inherits the publicly-known default credential shipped in the JS bundle. There is no server-side enforcement of a minimum or non-default password, making this a genuine default-credential risk for newly created accoun]

Password Reset Token Suffix Written to Audit Log — Audit log readers (admins or attackers who gain log access) can narrow token guessing attacks; reduces effective token entropy. [verified: Line 85 (the `summary` field passed to `record_audit`) stores `raw_token[-6:]` in the audit log, leaking the last 6 characters of a 43-character base64url token; while this alone does not enable account takeover, it materially reduces brute-force entropy for any attacker with audit log read access and constitutes genuine sensitive data exposure in logs.]

Security Headers Deliberately Disabled in frame endpoint — Removal of XSS and CSP protections allows script injection attacks to succeed without browser mitigation; amplifies the impact of any XSS vector. [verified: The `/ops/frame/tenant-slip-571` endpoint explicitly sets `X-XSS-Protection: 0` and `Content-Security-Policy: ''`, deliberately removing browser XSS mitigations for its responses. While gated by the ops token, this is a genuine deliberate security weakening with no compensating control.]

Security Headers Explicitly Disabled in /ops/frame Endpoint; No Security Headers on Main App — Browsers receive responses with XSS protection and CSP disabled, increasing susceptibility to XSS and clickjacking attacks. [verified: Duplicate of idx 15 — the `/ops/frame/tenant-slip-571` endpoint deliberately sets `X-XSS-Protection: 0` and `Content-Security-Policy: ''`; this is a confirmed deliberate security header removal with no compensating control, though impact is limited to ops-token-gated responses.]
